unit: Complete Chapter13: equations with prescribed singularities
status: All 35 original recursive inputs directly read; initial structural and introductory draft prepared. Both complete revised reads and all Chapter13 release checks remain pending.
findings: Declare X and dimension before the opening discussion; carry settings within regimes and make changes from semipositive big to arbitrary big backgrounds explicit.
Track reference type, capacity convergence, Holder inputs, scalar uniqueness and potential selection throughout all recursive inputs.

The root retains the semipositive model-reference condition in prescribed-type existence and the relative L-infinity estimate. Its convex pair construction uses common finite truncations, and the potentially nonuniform bounded-equivalence constant supplies only a genuine envelope.
The supersolution rooftop uses contact support of the model reference to eliminate its contribution; the prescribed-type existence proof is a separate nested input still to be read.

The positive-exponent closure theorem uses capacity convergence, an exponentially decaying tail, and L1 density convergence against a finite non-pluripolar measure. At exponent zero the uniform tail bound fails, so density convergence alone does not identify the potential measure.

The singular-domination opening calls the complementary background positive, although the proof uses a semipositive big form; clarify this regime on revision. Finite truncation sets justify all subtractions when total masses are infinite.

The bounded subsolution uses a convex transform of a strict singular potential and compensating polynomial density weight. Exponential solutions decrease with the approximating backgrounds. The normalized equation instead combines upper tail envelopes and lower finite rooftops, with an exponential weight identifying the common limit. Scalar uniqueness is retained separately from potential uniqueness.

The one-sided bounded stability proof truncates an unbounded comparison by max(v,u), solves a unit-Lq density problem on the strict excess set, treats zero and large restricted density norms separately, and optimizes the small-set estimate. Uniform convergence is used only after the limit equation is known.

The Hermitian Holder argument first converts L1 smoothing error through stability and the Kiselman transform, obtains a uniform lower bound on its minimizing radius, and then interpolates the uniform smoothing error with a gradient bound. The exponent alpha/(1+alpha) retains the strict endpoint.

Local continuity in a semipositive big background compensates curvature loss with a strict singular barrier. Uniform smoothing is only on sets where that barrier is bounded below; local Holder regularity is deferred to a separately proved rate.

Symmetry passes from unique positive-exponent solutions to normalized cluster solutions. The projective third solution is invariant under block exchange, while the two original smooth solutions are exchanged; this does not assert general zero-exponent uniqueness.

For the invariant projective solution, radial positivity gives a locally BV derivative. A primitive-flux identity survives convolution through signed bounded products; absence of atoms excludes jumps. The interior ODE, the first contact with the lower horizontal boundary, and boundedness at the projective ends determine the unique symmetric slope. Compactness then selects the entire normalized family.

Positive-exponent projective solutions have the same radial slope on the zero-density band as the selected limit; the slope is Lipschitz and has unequal one-sided derivatives at the two transition hypersurfaces. Smooth nonnegative density is not enough for C2 regularity.

Homogeneous local replacement uses smooth positive-density Dirichlet problems, uniform Lipschitz barriers for smooth boundary data, contraction for continuous data, and a strict upper-test argument for domination. It does not invoke global total-mass comparison.

Big-background contact support first proves continuity off a strict analytic barrier by regularization. Homogeneous replacement then localizes the envelope. Lower-semicontinuous competitors, quasi-continuous weights and signed finite truncations extend contact support without a finite-mass assumption.

Common lower barriers and a summable self-error give capacity convergence through finite rooftops and singular domination. The one-sided lower-barrier variant needs the limit to have the prescribed ordinary type. Fixed or moving dominating measures then provide raw tail control.

For the bounded subsolution theorem, smooth-density approximations have moving domination. The mixed density inequality and the fixed-reference trace bound control suprema even when positive lower bounds for the approximating densities vanish.

Weighted addition has an exponential error which absorbs the polynomial growth of truncated masses. The limiting equation is identified on finite levels with a fixed lower-barrier cutoff before taking the exhaustion.

Prescribed ordinary-type existence maximizes finite weighted mass between a nonzero supersolution measure and the datum. Compactness attains the maximum; weighted addition removes a proposed deficit. In the zero-exponent limit, upper comparison and the lower density norm control the scalar, without asserting potential uniqueness.

For arbitrary big backgrounds, local comparison uses the ordinary psh difference envelope and finite local positive measures. A strict analytic barrier confines the negative minimum to its regular locus. Reference-preserving subsolutions and the Gauduchon trace give estimates uniform in references between the barrier and zero.

Minimal-type exponential existence resolves strict analytic approximants. Disjoint first-contact partitions prevent a multiplicity factor in rooftop inequalities. Lower and upper monotone envelopes identify the limit. A uniform minimal-type interval then controls the vanishing-exponent scalar and density limits.

The interior smoothness opening must state strict positivity of the density and retain the entire regular locus of the fixed global barrier. The proof uses the proper gap, polynomial boundary trace bounds, exact approximation, subpower localization, C1-alpha convergence, polynomial Calabi estimates with torsion, and a nonlinear iteration to obtain a bounded trace.

The local density examples distinguish global regular-locus hypotheses from arbitrary local equations. The logarithmic continuous example has only L1 density; the accumulating-pole construction is bounded and discontinuous with constant local determinant; compact gluing locates the loss of every global Lp bound in the transition region. A separate Lipschitz example still fails C1 locally.

Resolved logarithmic types preserve Lp integrability on pullback with the bounded Jacobian. Residual positivity controls Holder regularity; mass formulas use closedness or the exact power conditions. Exceptional minimal types descend by the support theorem for closed order-zero differences and exceptional-fiber degree; Jacobians, not pole coefficients, determine the integrability exponents.

The measure-carrier section needs an explicit return to a general compact complex manifold after the blowup examples. Relative patching and a decreasing convex sum give absolute continuity against a sigma-finite extended measure, with an integrable density even if that reference measure has infinite mass.

Individual-density results distinguish positive scaled subsolutions, exact equations, scalar limits and capacity convergence. Bounded normalizers produce the obstruction at zero lower mass and the attained threshold. Smooth comparison tests can miss measurable concentrations; the constant test is legitimate because the chapter volume is a probability volume.

Gauduchon tests first have a uniform L2n bound, then extend to bounded roots and finally by monotone truncation to Ln. The endpoint root space is complete in the sum norm; upper and lower mass have different roles. Uniform tails characterize the closure of bounded roots but do not supply capacity convergence of potentials.

An exponential subsolution bounds decreasing truncated solutions below and gives a greatest exact positive-exponent solution. At positive threshold the scalars and right-hand measures converge; the root-tail modulus quantifies that convergence without establishing a general exact zero-exponent equation.
